newsitem.title: UK: Mark unable to make headway amid soft EMU concern.
newsitem.headline: Mark unable to make headway amid soft EMU concern.

text.p: The mark languished on its European crosses, unable to make headway amid speculation the planned European single currency will be softer and launched by a broader group of countries than Germany would like.

Expectations that France's opposition Socialist party are set to take power weighed on the mark as traders expect them to push for Italy and Spain to be included among the founding members of the single currency.

Sluggish growth is hampering Germany's bid to meet the Maastricht debt and deficit criteria, meantime, and reducing its ability to resist a more lenient interpretation of the Maastricht rules being applied.

"France is heading for a left-wing government which will be less pro-EMU than the previous one and Germany is fudging its books," said Teis Knuthsen, an international economist at First Chicago. "If people are convinced that EMU will go ahead but will be broader and softer than they'd thought, the mark should be softer."
Mark/Paris was last at 3.3768/73 from 3.3756/61 late Tuesday in Europe. Mark/lira was at 985.95/6.25 from 986.05/6.35 lire late yesterday.
It is not just France's opposition Socialist leader Lionel Jospin who has been talking of a broad EMU.

French National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, tipped as a possible contender for prime minister if the ruling centre-right coalition pull back in the polls, yesterday called for a looser euro and a more flexible approach to deciding EMU entrants.
One of the key beneficiaries of concern about monetary union will be the Swiss franc, traders said.

"People are looking to buy Swiss francs because of the uncertainty and the comments by Jospin and Seguin have also encouraged people to park money in the dollar," said a trader at a Japanese bank in London.

So far, the mark has been buoyed against the franc as traders expect the Swiss National Bank to continue to combat franc strength as its officials pledged to do in recent days. The SNB today added liquidity to the money-market at one percent for the second consecutive day.
Mark/Swiss was last at 83.37/39 centimes from 83.40/41 late yesterday.
Traders were sceptical, though, about how long this policy will succeed in keeping the franc in check.

"The Swiss franc will be the beneficiary of euro turmoil and the SNB will be moving against very large flows," he said. "They can play around with money-market rates but that won't do much about the fear and uncertainty which will be driving the market."

Monetary union was also a focus in Sweden. Swedish radio news Ekot cited sources as saying Prime Minister Goran Persson and Finance Minister Erik Asbrink do not want Sweden to join EMU in the next mandate period 1998-2002 without holding new parliamentary elections.

While the report initially undermined the crown, the Swedish currency pared its losses after government officials, including Asbrink, said the report was based on speculation. Mark/Swedish crown was last at 4.5050/80 from 4.4935/65 late yesterday in Europe.
